  "question": "A developer is refactoring a legacy monolithic application into microservices. They observe that while individual services now scale independently, the overall system throughput has decreased significantly under high concurrent load. Which architectural principle was most likely violated, causing this performance penalty?",
  "options": [
    "The services maintain a strict 1:1 mapping with the original database tables, preventing the optimization of data retrieval patterns.",
    "Synchronous HTTP calls were used to replace monolithic function calls, introducing network latency and requiring complex transaction management across service boundaries.",
    "The services were deployed on separate physical servers, causing CPU contention during load balancing operations.",
    "The internal state of each service is not persistent, leading to frequent re-initialization overhead when requests are routed to different instances."
  ],
  "correct_answer": 1,
  "explanation": "Refactoring from a monolith to microservices introduces network overhead. Using synchronous interactions (like REST/HTTP) for data retrieval that was previously a simple in-memory function call adds latency. If high-frequency inter-service calls are made synchronously, they can become a bottleneck. Understanding this trade-off (local function call vs. remote network call) is key to middleware performance, whereas the other options confuse state management or hardware specifics with the fundamental cost of distributed communication."
}
